Same Miles, Different Shape

Two build-ups to the Dallas Half Marathon, as told by my watch

On July 9, 2025, I went out in 87-degree rain and ran pyramid intervals because an app told me to. It was week one of an eight-week plan. I covered 4.2 miles at 9:18 a mile and felt every one of them.Everything here comes from my Strava log: 186 runs and 995 miles between that first run and 10 November 2026. Paces are moving pace.

Five months later I ran the Dallas Half Marathon in 1:38:08. Now I’m training for it again, five weeks out, with a broken leg somewhere in between. I wanted to know how this year’s build compares with last year’s, so I lined the two up.

Seventeen months, one dot per run

Each dot is a run, placed by date and distance. Hover over a dot for the details. The open circle is the race I haven’t run yet.The first build is easy to read. The dots climb from July to December, the long runs peel away from the weekday runs in September, and the whole thing ends at 13.1.

The second is messier. A mile time trial in January, a month of nothing in March while a leg healed, then a long flat stretch of five-mile runs through a Texas summer. The long runs only start to lift off in late September.

The balance is the same

A training block works a little like a savings account. You make deposits, and on race day you find out what the balance buys. So I added up the deposits, starting 22 weeks before each race.

Oddly though, despite the broken leg, the two accounts hold almost exactly the same amount. Five weeks out last year I had run 333 miles in 64 runs. Five weeks out this year: 331 miles in 63 runs. The gap is 2.3 miles, which is less than a warm-up.

The deposits are not

Last year I started from nothing and ramped hard. Weekly mileage tripled between July and November, and by five weeks out I had already gone past 12 miles 3 times, the last of them a full 13.

This year I started with a base and coasted on it. In the first thirteen weeks I banked 34 more miles than last year (218 against 183). In the five weeks since, I’ve given 37 of them back (113 against 149). The long run is the clearest difference: 11 miles is my longest so far, where last year it was 13.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. A half marathon doesn’t care much about the balance. It cares about the big deposits, and this year I haven’t made one over 11 miles.

What the heat costs

There is one thing in this year’s favor. My average pace is 9 seconds a mile quicker than at the same point last year, in weather that was, if anything, slightly hotter: 85 degrees on average against 83. In Dallas the thermometer does a lot of the pacing.

Across both years, every extra 10 degrees has cost me about 10 seconds a mile. The fitted line puts a 50-degree run at 8:14 and a 95-degree run at 8:59.This overstates the heat a little. My cool runs also come late in a build, when I’m fitter, so temperature is getting credit for some of the training. I haven’t tried to separate the two.

That makes me hypothesize that this year’s engine is at least as good as last year’s. The fastest efforts point the same way at the short end and the opposite way at the long end.

Last year’s 5K and 10K bests were both set inside the race itself. This year’s 5K came on an ordinary Tuesday morning run, the most recent one in the data.

What the race looked like

It is worth remembering what all those long runs bought. The first mile was the slowest at 8:34. Then I settled, and ran the back half much faster than the front: miles one through six averaged 7:50, miles eight through thirteen averaged 7:08. That is 42 seconds a mile quicker, with my heart rate pinned in the mid-160s for the last hour.

You can only run a second half like that if the distance itself is no longer a question. Last year, by race day, I had covered 13 miles or more three times in training.

Five weeks

In the last five weeks of the 2025 build I ran another 124 miles, race included, with long runs of 13, 13 and 14, and finished the block at 457. That is the part of the gray line the orange one hasn’t drawn yet.

The balance is fine. The next few Saturdays decide what it buys.

Data from Strava, last updated 10 November 2026. Charts are hand-built SVG; the data and the script that draws them are in Data/running.
